title: Manhwa Meta — Webtoon Episode Splash
description: A vertical-scroll-native slide built like a Naver Webtoon chapter opener: deep-ink silhouette, explosive Hangul onomatopoeia, and a brush-lettered episode title that makes every deck feel like a debut cut.
philosophy: This template refuses the horizontal corporate default and borrows the vertical rhythm of webtoon panels — a format tens of millions of Korean readers scan daily on mobile. It treats Hangul not as body copy but as a kinetic visual element, asserting that a single oversized '쾅' can carry more emotional charge than any bulleted list. It is designed for creators, brand storytellers, and educators speaking to audiences weaned on digital manhwa culture. It actively rejects symmetry, safe margins, and typographic restraint in favour of panel-energy and dramatic visual surprise.
goodFor: Episode-reveal splash slides in K-content or webtoon IP campaign decks
Chapter-opening hooks in youth-oriented educational or storytelling presentations
Brand launch moments targeting webtoon-native Gen-Z audiences
Single-statement hero slides featuring a character mascot or brand persona
avoidFor: Multi-column data tables or chart-heavy quarterly financial reviews
Formal government proposals, academic theses, or regulatory submissions
Landscape-only display environments locked to 16:9 corporate standard
Text-dense legal or compliance briefings requiring high information density
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide feels like the opening splash of a Naver Webtoon chapter — kinetic, ink-soaked, built for a reader who scrolls fast and stops hard. A towering character silhouette dominates the upper field, its edges dissolving into deep atmospheric shadow, while an oversized Hangul onomatopoeia erupts across the mid-frame like a panel impact line — more visual shockwave than typographic label. The mood is debut-night adrenaline: aggressively asymmetric, dramatically lit from a single raking angle, and wholly hostile to centered layouts, safe margins, or any softness that boardroom slides rely on.

examples.layoutNotes: Portrait-first canvas oriented for vertical scroll; a full-bleed silhouette graphic anchors the upper two-thirds with a hard-cropped diagonal edge that mimics a webtoon panel-break seam. The episode number or deck subtitle runs vertically along the left gutter in compact display weight, reinforcing the scroll-column feel. The primary title block crashes into the lower third at a slight oblique angle, flush-left with zero outer margin — intentionally kissing the frame edge. No header band, no footer rule; page identity is carried entirely by compositional drama.

examples.promptCore: This content slide lands like the second panel of a webtoon chapter — past the dramatic hook, now delivering the payload with kinetic confidence. The composition should feel asymmetric and deliberately restless, with oversized Hangul onomatopoeia erupting across panel gutters as a purely expressive visual force rather than readable copy. Content blocks behave like manhwa caption boxes — contained but charged, implying speed and narrative momentum. Avoid corporate calm, centered symmetry, or any airy whitespace that would dissolve the panel-energy tension.

examples.layoutNotes: Vertical 3-panel stacked layout with edge-to-edge bleed; the top panel spans full width as a deep-ink character or icon silhouette bleeding off both vertical edges. The middle panel holds the key statement or stat callout in an asymmetric left-heavy block, with an oversized Hangul onomatopoeia figure bursting rightward across the panel gutter. The bottom panel carries secondary copy or attribution flush-left, separated from the middle panel by a raw ink-line rule rather than whitespace. A webtoon-style episode counter sits outside the panel border at bottom-right as the sole navigational element.
